Archaeologists now believe this portly swine marks the oldest drawing of a creature yet discovered anywhere in the world. In a study published this week in Science Advances, an image of the drawing shows the animal apparently looking at two other pigs mid-squabble. pages.text: This ancient Greek warship ruled the Mediterranean | National Geographic By Arturo Sánchez Sanz Published February 23, 2023 • 13 min read Fast, maneuverable, and dangerous, the trireme was the most feared ship in ancient Greece. With powerful bronze rams and the ability to turn on a dime, it would leave enemy ships dead in the water by punching holes in their sides or smashing their oars. In his Histories , Herodotus writes how Greek naval dominance owed so much to the brilliant use of triremes in battle. ( This 3,500-year-old tomb held the treasures of Greece's 'Griffin Warrior'. ) In the fifth century B.C., Athenian shipyards had the capacity for over 300 triremes, the most famous warships of antiquity. The trireme—a term derived from the Greek trieres , “three rows of oars”—was the result of the continuous development of naval technology in the Greek world. The epic poem Iliad (attributed to Homer, and written in the eighth century B.C.) mentions ships called triaconters and penteconters , vessels that were crewed by 30 or 50 men, respectively. Biremes, with two rows of oarsmen, are recorded on eighth-century B.C. reliefs. At the beginning of the seventh century B.C., accumulated experience led to new technical advances, and the much more sophisticated trireme model appeared. Thucydides wrote that the Corinthians were the first to introduce the design to the Greek world, though modern historians think triremes may have first been built in Phoenicia, in the eastern Mediterranean and what is now Lebanon. Their build and claws have drawn comparisons to sloths, but some of these reptiles stood over 13 feet tall and weighed more than five tons. Now paleontologists have uncovered a therizinosaur that stands out even among its unusual relatives—because it’s missing a finger. While experimental brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have come a long way in being able to help them convey their thoughts , these technologies have generally been limited to either speech or movement . The implant, described in the journal Nature Neuroscience on September 14, allows users to control the speech and movement of a virtual avatar with their mind in real time. pages.description: A new study pushes back the advent of fire-making by more than quarter of a million years.
pages.text: This could be the oldest evidence of fire-making | National Geographic SCIENCE This could be the oldest evidence of fire-making A new study pushes back the advent of fire-making by more than quarter of a million years. Based on a pile of archaeological evidence, researchers think that Neanderthals were deliberately lighting fires as a site in England around 400,000 years ago. Artwork By Craig Williams © The Trustees of the British Museum By Tom Metcalfe Published December 10, 2025 Archaeologists have discovered what may be the earliest evidence of deliberate fire-making. At a site called East Farm in England, recent excavations revealed reddened silt, flint handaxes distorted by heat, and fragments of a mineral—iron pyrite—that could have been used to make sparks on tinder. Taken together, the finds suggest that an early group of Neanderthals deliberately and repeatedly set fires in a hearth there roughly 400,000 years ago. "In over 36 years of field work and geological studies in the area, we've never found pyrite before," says British Museum archaeologist Nick Ashton , the senior author of a study of the discoveries published in the journal Nature on December 10. "And now, the only time we find it is alongside heat-shattered handaxes and baked sediments." While the several distinct pieces of evidence make a strong case, figuring out if early humans lit flames on purpose is hard because the archaeological traces of natural and human-made fires look very similar. pages.description: An intense selection process and long preparation helped set the crew up for cohabitation in a 3D-printed replication of the Red Planet's environment in Houston. There, they practiced Marswalks, disrupted communications with people on Earth and food cultivation
pages.text: This Four-Person NASA Crew Spent Over a Year on 'Mars.' Here's What They Did for 378 Days in a Simulated Martian Habitat Skip to main content Four individuals participated in NASA's second Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) mission. NASA / James Blair On October 31, four NASA crewmembers returned from “Mars.” Not the actual Red Planet, of course, but a 3D-printed Mars habitat in Houston where the three men and one woman lived for 378 days. Now, the Mars analog astronauts— Ross Elder , Ellen Ellis , James Spicer and Matthew Montgomery —have started telling the world what took place after they disappeared into NASA’s Mars Dune Alpha habitat at the Johnson Space Center on October 19, 2025, for the agency’s second Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) mission. The mission aimed to test the kinds of physical and mental conditions that a team of Mars explorers would endure on the Red Planet, including long-term isolation, disrupted communication with people on Earth and food cultivation. The habitat includes both a base and a mock outdoor environment , so the crew could practice Marswalks. “For more than a year, they have lived in an isolated environment, conducting critical research and helping us better understand what it will take to send humans to Mars,” Vanessa Wyche , director of NASA’s Johnson Space Center, said during a livestream , just before the crew emerged. “Inside just 1,700 square feet, they managed to live with limited resources. They maintained their habitat. They grew crops, and they carried out simulated Mars operations.”

pages.text: This is the first ever confirmed skull of a Denisovan | National Geographic HISTORY & CULTURE Scientists discovered a new kind of human with its pinkie bone. Now we have a skull. Finally, we can put a face on a Denisovan. The "Dragon Man" skull was discovered in Harbin, China in 1933 by a local laborer, but remained hidden away until 2018. A new analysis now finds its very likely to be a Denisovan. Hundreds of the vessel’s treasures—including compasses, coins and cannonballs—have since surfaced on the beach. But Hughes was particularly intrigued by the lock. It looked like a dinosaur vertebra at first. But upon further inspection, researchers realized the bone was a curved, sword-like crest that would have been attached to the skull of one of paleontology’s most oddball dinosaurs—the sail-backed predator Spinosaurus . “It was amazing,” recalls Vidal, of the University of Chicago. “It was like a unicorn.” Back in 2022, when he stumbled upon the strange bone, he was part of a team led by National Geographic Explorer Paul Sereno, a paleontologist also at Chicago , excavating a remote fossil site called Jenguebi. After all, this is no ordinary water. What bubbles to the surface at Hot Springs National Park in Arkansas first fell as rain 4,000 years ago. Long before Hot Springs was designated a national park in 1921, Native tribes, including the Caddo, Quapaw, and Osage, were drawn to its steaming waters. This city lay a little to the south of where Cairo would be founded three centuries later. Al-Fusṭāṭ developed around a Roman fortress that had been seized from the Byzantines at the point where the Nile Valley fans out to form the delta. Were you to dig below Lyme Regis’ bunting-slung streets, you’d hit a geological marvel: the Blue Lias. This vast sequence of limestone and shale layers, formed during the Mesozoic era some 200 million years ago, reveals fossils as it erodes, making the town one of Europe’s most important paleontological centres. It’s a badge locals wear proudly: you’ll find a weather-beaten statue of celebrated fossil hunter Mary Anning overlooking Church Cliff Beach. In 1823, while wandering Lyme Regis’s coastline, she unearthed the world’s first complete skeleton of a Plesiosaurus and, nearly two centuries after her death, the town remains a magnet for excavators. The area is defined by a broad sagebrush sea, interspersed with juniper woodlands, rimrock, rolling rangelands, and seasonal and perennial streams and springs, reflecting the region’s Basin and Range geology and arid climate. Subtle elevation changes and gently undulating terrain shape a working landscape that supports both ecological diversity and traditional land uses. pages.text: Ticket Acceptance between participating Train Operators | National Rail Skip to main content Ticket Acceptance If your train journey is cancelled you can use your ticket 2 hours before or 2 hours after your original cancelled train with any participating Train Operator. If your train is cancelled, you will be able to travel on an alternative service operated by any other participating train operating company, listed below, either 2 hours before or 2 hours after the original departure time of the cancelled service, regardless of any train operator or route restriction shown on your ticket, in order to reach your destination. Customers must hold a valid ticket for their cancelled service, and this must have been purchased prior to the departure time of the cancelled service. Please note that this is only for cancelled services, not delays. In severe disruption where multiple cancellations occur, customers will be provided with additional information and advice on how to complete their journey. There may also be increased flexibility and it may be possible to use your ticket on a different part of the rail network with another train operator. Alternatively, when there are limited alternatives available or service disruption is severe, customers may be advised not to travel. In such cases, you are entitled to a full refund from your original point of sale if you choose not to travel or cannot complete your journey. pages.text: Tiger Woods set for competitive golf return in December's Hero World Challenge - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Tiger Woods has won 15 major titles - three behind Jack Nicklaus' record tally By Timothy Abraham , BBC Sport Journalist and Michael Emons , BBC Sport journalist Published 4 hours ago Tiger Woods is set to return to competitive golf in December for the first time in more than two years. Woods, 50, has not played in a traditional ranking event since the 2024 Open Championship at Royal Troon amid a series of off-course issues. The 15-time major champion has endured a challenging few years with a number of injuries and turmoil in his personal life. Woods will host next month's Hero World Challenge - an event which is part of the PGA Tour schedule but does not carry FedEx Cup points - and has been announced as part of the 20-player field. The American is one of three exemptions for the tournament in the Bahamas along with compatriots Rickie Fowler and Gary Woodland. Speaking to SiriusXM PGA Tour Radio in a video posted last week, Woods said: "I'm feeling better, no doubt about that. "I've been training quite a bit. I will be at Hero either way, so I'll see you there." Woods' long-awaited return comes after he accepted a five-year driving ban in September following a plea agreement in his reckless driving case. In March, Woods had been arrested and charged with driving under the influence after clipping a truck and rolling his car in Florida. These files include a variety of national and state-based geodatabases for geographic boundaries and features. These files do not include demographic data, but they contain geographic entity codes that can be linked to the Census Bureau’s demographic data, available on data.census.gov . Tim Bernardes: Tiny Desk Concert October 6, 2026 7:00 AM ET Anamaria Artemisa Sayre Credit: Photo: Elizabeth Gillis/NPR From jazz and Tejano to norteño and ska, 'El Tiny' returns with a takeover from Sept. 15 to Oct. 15 for Latin Music Month . "I will no longer carry the weight and burdens that aren't mine," Tim Bernardes coos behind the Desk. The Brazilian singer-songwriter sits easily in the poetry of the cosmos and his country, but communicates every emotion with tangible complexity. Alt.Latino Tim, The Beatles and all of Brazil Like so many great Brazilian artists, Bernardes translates hope and tragedy with the airiness of a butterfly but the precision of a surgeon. And beyond that, he integrates all of that sadness into his guitar. It's a wonder to watch him quite literally dance as he strums. By the time he's moved the feeling through, a revelation bursts through his chest: "I came here to live," he chants. There is always melancholy at the outset — Brazilians call this saudade — but in his confrontation and curiosity, Bernardes finds joy on the other side. Major Leap for Nuclear Clock Paves Way for Ultraprecise Timekeeping What are time and frequency? Time may be our most measured quantity — and unquestionably one of the most important. We use time to organize our lives, to communicate, to run global industries and to navigate our world. To keep time today, we use atoms — nature’s perfect clocks. Atoms themselves don’t tell time; rather, they absorb and emit specific frequencies of light waves. By building clocks that count those waves with exquisite accuracy, scientists can precisely measure and define the second — the fundamental unit of time — and share time with the world. The quest to accurately measure time and frequency has pushed the frontiers of science and opened up a host of technological applications. Some technologies, like GPS, are mature and used daily by billions of people. Photo by Brian Switek SCIENCE LAELAPS Time to Slay the T. rex Scavenger “Debate” Published July 16, 2013 • 11 min read Whether I’m on the radio, giving a public talk, or in conversation, one question about dinosaurs follows me almost everywhere I go – was Tyrannosaurus rex a mighty hunter or a lowly scavenger? I try to suppress my immediate urge to roll my eyes and despondently sigh whenever the query turns up. I’m not aggravated by the asker, but by the fact that a twenty year old non-debate has continued to create the impression of genuine controversy. The miscomprehension got another boost in the journal PNAS this week. The paper in question , composed by Palm Beach Museum of Natural History paleontologist Robert eePalma and coauthors, centers on a damaged tail bones from one of the herbivorous, shovel-beaked hadrosaurs that roamed western North America around 66 million years ago. Tucked inside a rounded, ugly mass of pathological bone fusing two vertebrae is the tip of a tooth from a large carnivorous dinosaur – most likely the infamous T. rex given the anatomy of the tooth and the lack of other large predators in the same geologic formation. Such damage, dePalma and colleagues rightly conclude, was probably caused by a failed attempt to take down the hadrosaur. May 15, 2024 Español Tips for Traveling With Diabetes Key points Traveling gets you out of your normal diabetes routine. Delayed meals, unfamiliar foods, different time zones, and changes to activity can all impact your blood sugar. But diabetes management doesn't have to go on vacation just because you do. Before you go Stay up to date on regular doctor's visits to be sure you're fit to travel. Find out how to adjust your medicines for different time zones and eating schedules, or how to get refills if needed. While packing , put your diabetes supplies (medicine, blood sugar monitor, etc.) and healthy snacks where you can get to them easily, like in your carry-on bag if you are flying. Pack twice as much medicine as you think you'll need. If you're going through security at the airport there's good news: people with diabetes can bring over 3.4 ounces of liquids through security in their carry-ons. This allows them to travel with liquid medicines, fast-acting sugar sources like juice, or gel packs to keep insulin cool. Finally, be aware that insulin pumps or continuous glucose monitors (CGMs) could be damaged by X-ray machines.

pages.description: Half a century after its inception, the Coast to Coast path becomes a National Trail this spring, opening up the wild landscapes and historic villages of Northern England to a new generation of hikers.
pages.text: To see the best of rural England, hike the Coast to Coast trail | National Geographic By Duncan Craig Published March 2, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Engulfed by their changing robes and cradling mugs of hot chocolate, the two swimmers seem admirably oblivious to the gusting wind barrelling off the Irish Sea. The pebble-backed beach on which they stand is still varnished from high tide and so expansive it renders the adjacent hamlet an inconsequential footnote. This is St Bees, on the unheralded Cumbrian coast, where the Lake District’s fells finally run out of puff and collapse into a supine, soporific coastal band. Offshore is the spiky-backed silhouette of the Isle of Man. It’s an arresting spot but, for the next six days, a different, distant shoreline is my focus. Leaving the beach, I set off up the steep headland path. In my hand is a small, grey, pleasingly smooth pebble taken from the beach. All being well, as is the custom, I’ll be depositing this in a little under a week’s time in the restless grey waters of the North Sea. Author Alfred Wainwright was nearing his dotage when he drew on his unrivalled experience of hiking in his native Northern England to publish an illustrated guide entitled A Coast to Coast Walk in 1973. ‘I want to encourage the ambition in others to devise their own cross-country marathons,’ he wrote. So brilliantly conceived and artfully evoked was his trail — from St Bees through the heart of Lakeland, the Yorkshire Dales and on to the North York Moors — it became an instant hit. pages.text: To solve the mysteries of Homo naledi, he returned to the ‘cave of bones’ | National Geographic Premium HISTORY & CULTURE He returned to the ‘cave of bones’ to solve the mysteries of human origins To unearth the secrets of an ancient human relative, paleoanthropologist Lee Berger had to squeeze through a chute seven and a half inches wide—the length of a pencil. Fossils from the Rising Star cave system surround the skeleton of Homo naledi. Considering the primitive core but human-like extremities, “it’s like evolution is crafting us from the outside in,” says paleoanthropologist John Hawks. Photograph by Robert Clark By Lee Berger Published June 5, 2023 • 20 min read “I think we should stop the excavation,” I said. As I gestured at the ghostly image on the computer screen, I looked over at Keneiloe Molopyane, an archaeologist and forensic scientist known on our team as Bones. We were watching a live stream of two colleagues, archaeologists Marina Elliott and Becca Peixotto, digging around a hundred feet beneath us. Bones leaned in to look at the screen as the light from the excavators’ head lamps darted around the chamber. “Why stop?” she asked. It was November 2018, and we were sitting at our team’s “command center” in South Africa’s Rising Star cave system, which comprises nearly two and a half miles of interlaced passages, descending in some places more than 130 feet underground. Todd Brinson Todd Brinson elected to pursue a career in civil service after retiring from the military where he spent 17 of 20 years serving in the Special Operations community. Prior to his role as the IM-60 Deputy CIO, he served as the Director of the Customer Advocacy and IT Service Management Office. Todd has over 15 years’ experience helping Federal CIOs develop and deliver cost effective, resilient, and secure services to meet customer needs. Specializing in IT Service Delivery, Todd uses that experience to build relationships with customers to understand their pain points and co-create services that meet their Use and Utility expectations. Todd earned his Master of Project Management (M.P.M.) at Penn State and he has been able to apply this specialized knowledge to planning and executing IT Services to meet customer’s needs successfully. Over the years, his strengths at the Department of Energy have garnered recognition for completing multiple highly visible and complex initiatives, despite being introduced to unconventional challenges.

He has also served as the Division Director for Financial Policy within the Office of the CFO and a Risk Management Analyst for the Office of Acquisition Management with responsibilities for internal controls, audit resolution, and financial assistance policy. Tommy Joyce Tommy Joyce Tommy Joyce serves as NNSA's Associate Administrator for Strategic Partnerships, where he is a principal executive advisor to the Administrator and the Principal Deputy Administrator. pages.text: Toppled trees force Newton Stewart fixture postponement Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Toppled trees force football fixture postponement 27 October 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Newton Stewart FC A tree fell through a perimeter fence and was left hanging over the pitch Toppled trees have forced the postponement of a match in Scottish football's fifth tier on player and spectator safety grounds. Newton Stewart were scheduled to host Gretna 2008 at Blairmount Park in the Lowland League West but the club posted pictures of the scale of the problem being faced. One tree had caused significant damage to a perimeter fence and was lying over the pitch. The club said it was being removed but it needed to get a professional assessment of other trees nearby with high winds expected throughout the day. Newton Stewart FC Safety checks will be carried out at the ground The area around the ground has seen "significant damage" in the past few days due to storms sweeping across the country. The club warned anyone heading up to the area that it might be unsafe until a proper assessment was carried out. At the weekend fallen trees blocked the entrance to the ground and now more have come down next to the pitch. The one overhanging the pitch has been removed but further assessment will be carried out by experts to see if there is a risk of further damage. pages.text: Tori Kelly: Tiny Desk Concert : NPR Accessibility links Skip to main content Keyboard shortcuts for audio player Tori Kelly: Tiny Desk Concert Not only does Tori Kelly fill the Tiny Desk with her commanding voice but also genuine joy and light. Tori Kelly: Tiny Desk Concert September 10, 2026 5:00 AM ET Ashley Pointer Credit: Photo: Michael Zamora/NPR When Tori Kelly pulled up to the Desk, her band already mid-rehearsal, she immediately got to work and filled our room with her commanding voice. She had arrived. And with her, she carried genuine joy and light. Backed by an all-woman band of Tiny Desk alumnae, Kelly effortlessly moves through songs from her latest album, God Must Really Love Me . The record captures Kelly in the present: reflecting on her faith journey and navigating life as a new mom. She also drops some gems for the day one's, including brief tastes of "Nobody Love" and "Dear No One." But, most serendipitously for the middle schoolers in attendance, Kelly performs her rendition of Stevie Wonder 's "Don't You Worry 'Bout a Thing," the song that her character Meena belts in the animated film Sing . Sponsor Message I've always found Tori Kelly to be inspiring. Beyond her anointing as a vocalist and musician, she has endured the many shifts of the music industry while maintaining an authenticity that cuts through the noise and reaches the heart. There's something special about watching an artist who has grown so much, yet still sounds and feels unmistakably like herself. Tortas for all sizes, baked by my family on Christmas Eve. Photo by Jane Dulay For the majority of the year, I am half Filipina, far distanced from cultural traditions that began fading when my grandparents uprooted the family from their homeland. But during Christmas, I try to embrace this identity fully through a few small rituals. Every year we hang our párol star lantern in the front window, we let Nana say grace before eating chicken adobo and pancit , and we bake torta . I remember my mom showing me when I was young how to cut the scalloped edges of the paper and carefully fill the ridges of the pans. pages.text: Tottenham Hotspur FC - Transfer news, results, fixtures, video and audio Tottenham Hotspur Latest updates Image source, Getty Images So, in Harry Kane, England has its first Ballon d'Or winner in 25 years. And the newly-crowned world's best player was made in Tottenham. Kane joined Spurs' academy in 2009 and rose through the ranks, including spending loan spells at Leyton Orient, Millwall, Norwich City and Leicester City, making his debut in 2011 and eventually breaking into the first team regularly under Tim Sherwood in 2014. His first opportunities for Spurs came in the Europa League, and on the day he scored his first senior hat-trick in a group stage win over Asteras Tripolis, he ended the game in goal after Hugo Lloris was sent off. Kane became the club's greatest-ever goalscorer, and now the first-ever player to come through the club's academy and go on to win the Ballon d'Or. In his acceptance speech on Monday, Kane said: "I want to say thank you to Tottenham Hotspur, as well. I wouldn't be where I am today without Tottenham, for sure. "I was there from 11 years old. All the guidance, the coaches - you allowed me to live my dream. So, for sure, without all those moments together, all the ups and down along the way of that journey has led me to this moment here today. "So I just want to say thank you to Tottenham Hotspur." Kane also put on record his thanks to a number of his coaches who trained him from his early days in Spurs' academy, as well as key figures at the club. "I want to give a shout-out to some of my coaches that have helped me along the way," he added.

pages.text: Tottenham Hotspur FC - Transfer news, results, fixtures, video and audio Tottenham Hotspur Latest updates Image source, PA Media Former England captain Wayne Rooney, speaking on The Wayne Rooney Show about Tottenham's 3-0 loss to Nottingham Forest: "Getting positive results against Liverpool and Atletico Madrid, it felt like they were getting back on track - then to play the team you're fighting against relegation at home and lose 3-0 is an absolute nightmare. "Obviously, West Ham losing helps them a little bit, but it couldn't have been a worse day for Tottenham. "You think only a few years ago they were in the Champions League final and won the Europa League last season. To be on the brink of getting relegated is an absolute disaster. I can't believe they're down there, to be honest." On the battle for Premier League survival: "One win changes everything. One win brings Leeds and Forest back into it. "[Of Spurs' remaining opponents] they could beat any of them on their day. I think the big thing is confidence. We've seen in the last week, they get a point at Anfield and then beat Atletico. "A lot is on confidence and belief, not just from the players, but from the fans as well, and that just seems to be as low as it can get at the minute." pages.text: Tottenham Hotspur FC - Transfer news, results, fixtures, video and audio Tottenham Hotspur Latest updates Paul Birch BBC Sport journalist Tottenham go in search of a first league win of the season against a Coventry City side who have roared into form with back-to-back victories. BBC Sport takes a look at some of the key themes going into Monday's fixture. Can Tottenham banish home woes to record a first victory? In the wake of their draw with Manchester United , Tottenham headed to Marbella for a few days of warm weather training and, more importantly, squad bonding. "The target is to build the team," head coach Roberto de Zerbi explained. "We are a great group of players, but we are not a team yet." His side certainly looked like more of a cohesive unit at Old Trafford, but their slick approach play was squandered by yet more profligacy in front of goal as their winless start stretched to six league matches. Only two top-flight sides have completed more passes in the final third than Spurs' 770 and just three teams have had more touches in the opposition box than their 182. Yet a shot conversion rate of 3.6% is the worst in the league and De Zerbi's side have underperformed their xG by 3.6 goals. Three goals after six league matches is the second lowest tally in their history, beaten only by the two scored at the start of 2006-07. They are still yet to lead in a league match this season or score a goal before the 86th minute. One thing they still cannot count on is home comforts.
